claims.feature: other: competing memories of one event
claims.claim: Malosse notes that the scene he cites to show Kay's style is presented as a senator's memory of what happened in front of him.
claims.source: Pierre-Louis Malosse, Université Paul Valéry, Anabases 5 (2007)
claims.quote: A senator, Plautus Bonosus, remembers the scene as it unfolded before him

claims.claim: Malosse offers one passage as the sample by which to judge Kay's style against the narrative Procopius supplies.
claims.source: Pierre-Louis Malosse, Université Paul Valéry, Anabases 5 (2007)
claims.quote: a passage to provide a sense of Guy Gavriel Kay’s style

claims.claim: Patton describes Kay laying narrative episodes next to each other in a lapidary fashion, sometimes making neighbours of vastly different places, ranks and perspectives.
claims.source: Andrew Patton, artist and art critic, in a Sarantine Letters essay written inside an in-world scholarly conceit
claims.quote: the lapidary fashion in which narratival episodes were laid next to each other

claims.claim: Patton urges attention to the construction of Kay's book at the scale of the sentence as well as of the episode.
claims.source: Andrew Patton, artist and art critic, in a Sarantine Letters essay written inside an in-world scholarly conceit
claims.quote: in both the writing of sentences and the composing of separate episodes

claims.claim: Campbell argues that Kay's shift into a more formal register for one episode of The Summer Tree adds mythic gravitas to that section.
claims.source: Narelle Campbell, PhD thesis, University of Wollongong (2013)
claims.quote: further mythic gravitas to this section of Kay’s tale.
claims.page: c. p. 322, chapter on Diarmuid and Sharra

claims.claim: Campbell argues that the mythic ambience and literary resonance of The Fionavar Tapestry obscure the ethnic and gender imbalances of the episode in which Diarmuid seduces Sharra.
claims.source: Narelle Campbell, PhD thesis, University of Wollongong (2013)
claims.page: chapter on Diarmuid and Sharra, paragraph beginning 'the plausibility of newer stories'

claims.claim: Rettino argues that when the narrator's voice reveals itself in Tigana it takes on the authority of a club-story teller.
claims.quote: When the narrator’s voice reveals itself, it adopts the authority of the club-story teller
claims.page: section on Tigana and the club-story

claims.claim: Rettino argues that Kay's omniscient narrator in Under Heaven subverts historical narration by revealing that many events in history are not known.
claims.quote: by revealing that many events in history are not known

claims.claim: Kay said in 1989 that if he rewrote The Fionavar Tapestry he would polish the prose of the opening chapters.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, interviewed by Raymond H. Thompson at Mythcon, Vancouver, 30 July 1989 (The Camelot Project, 1999)
claims.quote: I might polish the prose itself
claims.page: answer to 'If you could wave a magic wand that would rewrite the book'

claims.claim: Ordway frames her study as an account of how Kay invests a secondary world with the consistency of reality.
claims.source: Holly E. Ordway, UMass Amherst independent study (1998)
claims.quote: investing it with the consistency of reality

claims.feature: other: sources of a secondary world
claims.claim: Ordway states that Kay draws on literature, mythology and history as well as his own imagination to build his worlds.
claims.source: Holly E. Ordway, UMass Amherst independent study (1998)
claims.quote: draws on literature, mythology, and history as well as his own imagination

claims.claim: Webb argues that in Tigana the major events have their genesis in the emphatically freely willed actions of the protagonists.
claims.source: Janeen Webb, The Ringbearer: Journal of the Mythopoeic Literature Society of Australia (1991)
claims.quote: the major events have their genesis in the emphatically freely willed actions
claims.page: section on mythology and human deeds

claims.feature: other: memory and the erased name
claims.claim: Doshlova argues that Tigana's central metaphors — the lost name, distorted memory and music — form a single artistic system representing the formation, loss and recovery of national identity.
claims.source: M. R. Doshlova, Kuban State University, conference paper (Ural Federal University archive)

claims.claim: Palmatier says the Italian flavour of Tigana's invented world is carried by its word structure, place names and characters.
claims.source: Joshua Palmatier (novelist), 'Altering the Familiar: Tigana by Guy Gavriel Kay', Reactor/Tor.com 'That Was Awesome! Writers on Writing', 2016
claims.quote: the flavor of Italy is there—in the word structure, the place names

claims.claim: Palmatier disputes the common view that Kay's art lies in his use of language, locating it instead in the alteration of a familiar setting.
claims.source: Joshua Palmatier (novelist), 'Altering the Familiar: Tigana by Guy Gavriel Kay', Reactor/Tor.com 'That Was Awesome! Writers on Writing', 2016
claims.quote: not in the use of language, but in the subtle way
